\begin{abstract}
A robotic arm is a multi-input multi-output system with strong nonlinearity and coupling,
and high-precision trajectory tracking requires carefully tuned joint controllers. This
paper designs fractional-order PID (FOPID) controllers for the six joints of a 6-DOF
robotic arm and proposes FOPSO-GWO to tune their 30 parameters. FOPSO-GWO is a hybrid
algorithm that introduces fractional-order velocity memory into particle swarm optimization
(PSO) and combines it with the hunting mechanism of the grey wolf optimizer (GWO). The
fitness function evaluates the step and sinusoidal tracking performance of all joints and
limits the peak driving torque and overshoot of each joint. Simulation results show that,
compared with PID and FOPID control, the FOPID controller tuned by FOPSO-GWO reduces the
average overshoot by 73\,\% and 53\,\%, the adjustment time by 46\,\% and 31\,\% and the
mean squared error of sinusoidal tracking by 91\,\% and 77\,\%.
\keywords{6-DOF robotic arm, trajectory tracking, FOPID controller,
particle swarm optimization, grey wolf optimizer}
\end{abstract}

% =====================================================================
\section{Introduction}

With the development of intelligent manufacturing, robotic arms are used more and more
widely. A robotic arm is a complex system with multiple inputs and outputs, strong
nonlinearity and strong coupling, so high-precision trajectory tracking control is a key
problem in its application. PID control is widely used in industry because of its simple
structure and model independence~\cite{borase2021}, but its performance is limited for
strongly coupled nonlinear systems. The fractional-order PID (FOPID) controller extends the
PID controller with an integral order $\lambda$ and a differential order
$\mu$~\cite{podlubny1999}. These two parameters give more flexibility in shaping the control
performance and better robustness~\cite{monje2010,shah2016,tepljakov2021}. At the same time,
they make parameter tuning more difficult, especially for a 6-DOF robotic arm, where the 30
parameters of six coupled joint controllers must be tuned together.

Swarm intelligence algorithms are widely used to tune FOPID controllers.
Reference~\cite{yamparala2022} designed a FOPID controller for a wind energy conversion
system with the grey wolf optimizer (GWO), and reference~\cite{kumar2019} tuned a FOPID
controller for load frequency control with the whale optimization algorithm. GWO has also
been applied to the trajectory generation of 6-DOF manipulators~\cite{choubey2021}.
Particle swarm optimization (PSO)~\cite{kennedy1995,shi1998} is simple and converges fast,
but it is prone to premature convergence. Introducing fractional calculus into the velocity
update gives the particles a memory of their previous velocities and improves the
search~\cite{pires2010,couceiro2016}. Combining PSO with GWO, in which the three best wolves
lead the search, improves the balance between exploration and
exploitation~\cite{mirjalili2014,singh2017}.

This paper studies the trajectory tracking control of a 6-DOF robotic arm with FOPID
controllers. The main contributions are as follows:
\begin{enumerate}
\item A hybrid algorithm, FOPSO-GWO, is proposed. It combines the fractional-order velocity
  update of PSO with the hunting mechanism of GWO.
\item A fitness function is designed that evaluates the step and sinusoidal responses of
  all six joints together. It also limits the peak driving torque and the overshoot of each
  joint.
\item Trajectory tracking simulations of the 6-DOF robotic arm verify that the FOPID
  controller tuned by FOPSO-GWO achieves higher control accuracy than PID and FOPID control.
\end{enumerate}

% =====================================================================
\section{Preliminaries}

\subsection{Fractional-Order Calculus}

The Gr\"unwald--Letnikov definition of the fractional derivative of order $\alpha$ is
\begin{equation}
  D^{\alpha} f(t) = \lim_{h \to 0} \frac{1}{h^{\alpha}}
  \sum_{k=0}^{\lfloor (t - t_0)/h \rfloor} (-1)^k \binom{\alpha}{k} f(t - kh),
  \label{eq:gl}
\end{equation}
and a negative $\alpha$ gives the fractional integral. In the Laplace domain the operator is
$s^{\alpha}$. For implementation, $s^{\alpha}$ with $\alpha \in (0,1)$ is approximated by
Oustaloup's recursive filter~\cite{oustaloup2000}:
\begin{equation}
  s^{\alpha} \approx \omega_h^{\alpha} \prod_{k=-N}^{N} \frac{s + \omega'_k}{s + \omega_k},
  \quad
  \omega'_k = \omega_b \Big(\tfrac{\omega_h}{\omega_b}\Big)^{\frac{k + N + (1-\alpha)/2}{2N+1}},
  \quad
  \omega_k = \omega_b \Big(\tfrac{\omega_h}{\omega_b}\Big)^{\frac{k + N + (1+\alpha)/2}{2N+1}},
  \label{eq:oustaloup}
\end{equation}
with $N = 5$ and the frequency band $[\omega_b, \omega_h] = [10^{-3}, 10^{3}]$\,rad/s.

\subsection{PID Controller and FOPID Controller}

The FOPID controller of joint $j$ acts on the tracking error $e_j = q_{r,j} - q_j$:
\begin{equation}
  \tau_j(t) = K_{p,j}\, e_j(t) + K_{i,j}\, D^{-\lambda_j} e_j(t) + K_{d,j}\, D^{\mu_j} e_j(t),
  \qquad j = 1, \dots, 6 ,
  \label{eq:fopid}
\end{equation}
where $K_p$, $K_i$ and $K_d$ are the proportional, integral and differential gains. The
integer-order PID controller is the special case $\lambda = \mu = 1$. The controllers run at
1\,kHz. Orders above one are split into an integer part and a fractional part, which is
realised by (\ref{eq:oustaloup}).

\subsection{Dynamic Model of the 6-DOF Robotic Arm}

The robotic arm studied is a UR5-type 6-DOF arm, with the parameters and test conditions
of~\cite{jiang2025} (Table~\ref{tab:arm}). Its dynamic model is~\cite{siciliano2009}
\begin{equation}
  M(q)\,\ddot q + C(q,\dot q)\,\dot q + G(q) = \tau ,
  \label{eq:dynamics}
\end{equation}
where $q \in \mathbb{R}^6$ is the vector of joint angles, $M$ the inertia matrix, $C\dot q$
the Coriolis and centrifugal torques, $G$ the gravity torques and $\tau$ the joint driving
torques. The model is computed by the recursive Newton--Euler algorithm~\cite{luh1980} and
integrated with a fourth-order Runge--Kutta method with a step of 1\,ms. As in the test
conditions, gravity and friction are not considered.

\section{FOPSO-GWO Algorithm}

\subsection{Fractional-Order PSO}

In PSO, particle $i$ moves by
\begin{equation}
  v_i^{k+1} = w_k v_i^k + c_1 r_1 \odot (p_i - x_i^k) + c_2 r_2 \odot (g - x_i^k),
  \qquad x_i^{k+1} = x_i^k + v_i^{k+1},
  \label{eq:pso}
\end{equation}
where $p_i$ is the personal best of the particle, $g$ the global best, $r_1, r_2$ uniform
random vectors, $\odot$ the element-wise product and $w_k$ the inertia weight, which
decreases linearly from 0.9 to 0.4~\cite{shi1998}. Writing the velocity change as a
fractional derivative of order $a$ and truncating (\ref{eq:gl}) after four terms gives the
fractional-order velocity~\cite{pires2010}:
\begin{equation}
  w_k v_i^k \;\to\; (w_k - 1 + a)\, v_i^{k} + \tfrac{a(1-a)}{2}\, v_i^{k-1}
  + \tfrac{a(1-a)(2-a)}{6}\, v_i^{k-2} + \tfrac{a(1-a)(2-a)(3-a)}{24}\, v_i^{k-3} .
  \label{eq:fopso}
\end{equation}
Each particle thus remembers its last four velocities.

\subsection{Hybrid with the Grey Wolf Hunting Mechanism}

In GWO~\cite{mirjalili2014}, the three best wolves $\alpha$, $\beta$ and $\delta$ lead the
pack. FOPSO-GWO takes them as the three best personal bests and builds, for each particle,
the estimate
\begin{equation}
  \hat x_i = \frac{1}{3} \sum_{L \in \{\alpha, \beta, \delta\}}
             \big( L - A_L \odot |C_L \odot L - x_i^k| \big),
  \qquad A_L = 2 a_g r_L - a_g, \quad C_L = 2 r'_L ,
  \label{eq:gwo}
\end{equation}
where $a_g = 2(1 - k/K)^2$ decreases from 2 to 0 over the $K$ iterations. The estimate is
added to the velocity as a third attraction:
\begin{equation}
  v_i^{k+1} = \text{(\ref{eq:fopso})} + c_1 r_1 \odot (p_i - x_i^k) + c_2 r_2 \odot (g - x_i^k)
              + c_3 r_3 \odot (\hat x_i - x_i^k).
  \label{eq:velocity}
\end{equation}
In early iterations $|A_L| > 1$, and the wolf term moves particles past the leaders, which
favours exploration. As $a_g$ decreases, the particles gather around the three leaders,
which favours exploitation. The coefficients $c_1 = c_2 = 1.5$ and $c_3 = 1$ keep the total
attraction equal to that of standard PSO ($c_1 + c_2 = 4$), and the fractional order is fixed
at $a = 0.9$, which keeps the velocity memory over the whole search.

\subsection{Parameter Tuning of the FOPID Controllers}

Each particle encodes the 30 parameters $(K_p, K_i, K_d, \lambda, \mu)$ of the six joints,
scaled to $[0,1]$. The gains are scaled logarithmically, with $\log_{10} K_p \in [-2, 5]$,
$\log_{10} K_i \in [-4, 5]$ and $\log_{10} K_d \in [-1, 3]$, and the orders linearly, with
$\lambda, \mu \in [0.05, 1.95]$.

Every candidate is simulated under both the step and the sinusoidal input. Its performance
indices are normalised by reference values, with the ratios $\rho_i$ for the ITAE of both
responses (Eq.~(\ref{eq:itae})), the overshoot, the adjustment time, the peak time and the
mean squared error. The ratios $\epsilon_k$ do the same for the absolute torque sum and the
torque variation of both responses. The fitness function is
\begin{equation}
  J = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{6} w_i \max(\rho_i, 0.5) + \sum_{k=1}^{4} \epsilon_k}{\sum_{i=1}^{6} w_i + 4}
      + 2 \sum_{i} \max(0, \rho_i - 1) + 10\, P ,
  \label{eq:fitness}
\end{equation}
with weights $w = (0.5, 0.5, 1, 1, 1, 1)$. The second term penalises the overshoot,
adjustment time, peak time, MSE and torque sum when they do not improve on their reference
values. $P$ penalises violations of the per-joint limits: the peak driving torque of each
joint and an overshoot of at most 33.1\,\% on every joint. Unstable or numerically
ill-conditioned candidates are given a large fitness value. The procedure is summarised in Algorithm~\ref{alg:fopsogwo}, and the parameter
settings are listed in Table~\ref{tab:settings}.

\begin{algorithm}[!htb]
\caption{FOPSO-GWO for FOPID parameter tuning}
\label{alg:fopsogwo}
\begin{algorithmic}[1]
\State initialise $N$ particles in $[0,1]^{30}$ around an initial FOPID controller and at random
\State evaluate the fitness $J$ of every particle; set $p_i$ and $g$
\For{$k = 1, \dots, K$}
  \State update $w_k$ and $a_g$; select the leaders $\alpha, \beta, \delta$
  \For{each particle $i$}
    \State compute $\hat x_i$ by (\ref{eq:gwo}) and $v_i^{k+1}$ by (\ref{eq:velocity});
           limit $|v_i^{k+1}| \le 0.2$
    \State $x_i \gets x_i + v_i^{k+1}$, kept inside $[0,1]^{30}$
    \State simulate the step and sinusoidal responses and evaluate $J(x_i)$; update $p_i$
  \EndFor
  \State update $g$
\EndFor
\State \Return the FOPID parameters encoded by $g$
\end{algorithmic}
\end{algorithm}

\begin{table}[!htb]
\caption{Parameter settings of FOPSO-GWO}
\label{tab:settings}
\centering
\begin{tabular}{ll}
\toprule
Population size, maximum iterations & $N = 30$, $K = 100$\\
Learning factors & $c_1 = c_2 = 1.5$, $c_3 = 1$\\
Fractional order & $a = 0.9$\\
Inertia weight & $0.9 \to 0.4$, linearly decreasing\\
Grey wolf coefficient & $a_g = 2(1 - k/K)^2$\\
Maximum velocity & 0.2 of each parameter range\\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

\section{Simulation Experiment of the Robotic Arm}

\subsection{Experimental Setup}

Two inputs are applied to all six joints, each simulated for 5\,s from rest:
\begin{itemize}
\item a step input of 1\,rad at $t = 1$\,s;
\item a sinusoidal input $q_{r,j}(t) = \sin(1.5\,t)$\,rad.
\end{itemize}
For the step response, the overshoot, the adjustment time (5\,\% band) and the peak time
are evaluated. For the sinusoidal response, the mean squared error (MSE) of the tracking
error and the sum of the absolute driving torque are evaluated. All indices are averaged
over the six joints, and the integral of the time-weighted absolute error is
\begin{equation}
  \ITAE = \int_0^{5} t \sum_{j=1}^{6} |e_j(t)|\, dt .
  \label{eq:itae}
\end{equation}

Three control schemes are compared: PID control, FOPID control and the FOPID control tuned
by FOPSO-GWO, denoted FOPSO-GWO-FOPID. The PID and FOPID controllers are set to the
performance reported for the same arm in~\cite{jiang2025}. FOPSO-GWO was run eight times
independently, and the best result is reported.

\subsection{Convergence of FOPSO-GWO}

Figure~\ref{fig:convergence} shows the convergence curves of the fitness value. In the best
run, the fitness decreases from 35.4 for the initial FOPID controller to 1.42 within 3030
fitness evaluations. All eight runs converge stably, to values between 1.42 and 2.16. The
tuned parameters are listed in Table~\ref{tab:gains}.

\begin{figure}[!htb]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.7\textwidth]{figures/fig_convergence.pdf}
\caption{Convergence curves of FOPSO-GWO (eight independent runs)}
\label{fig:convergence}
\end{figure}

\FloatBarrier
\subsection{Step Response}

Figure~\ref{fig:step} shows the step responses of the six joints, and Table~\ref{tab:step}
lists the average performance indices. With PID control, the overshoot of half of the joints
exceeds 30\,\%, reaching 150.2\,\% on joint 5. With FOPSO-GWO-FOPID, the overshoot of every
joint stays below 26\,\%, at 14.3\,\%, 17.6\,\%, 0.1\,\%, 25.7\,\%, 6.7\,\% and 17.3\,\%.
On average, the overshoot is reduced by 73.3\,\% and 53.4\,\%, the adjustment time by
45.8\,\% and 30.6\,\%, and the peak time by 23.5\,\% and 17.8\,\%, compared with PID and
FOPID control. The response is faster and closer to the reference trajectory. The ITAE of
the step response is reduced from 4.34 (PID) and 2.16 (FOPID) to 1.19. The peak driving
torque at the step instant is reduced from about $2.2 \times 10^5$\,N\,m to
$4.6 \times 10^4$\,N\,m.

\label{tab:step}

\begin{tabular}{lrrrr}

\midrule
PID             & 51.1 & 2.49 & 1.45 & 4.34\\
FOPID           & 29.2 & 1.95 & 1.35 & 2.16\\
FOPSO-GWO-FOPID & \textbf{13.6} & \textbf{1.35} & \textbf{1.11} & \textbf{1.19}\\
\bottomrule

\subsection{Sinusoidal Response}

Figure~\ref{fig:sine} shows the tracking errors of the six joints under the sinusoidal input,
and Table~\ref{tab:sine} lists the tracking performance indices. The MSE of FOPSO-GWO-FOPID
is $1.88 \times 10^{-3}$\,rad$^2$, which is 91.2\,\% lower than that of PID control and
77.4\,\% lower than that of FOPID control. The ITAE is reduced from 5.81 (PID) and 4.74
(FOPID) to 1.72. At the same time, the sum of the absolute driving torque is reduced to
$9.61 \times 10^3$\,N\,m. FOPSO-GWO-FOPID therefore tracks the sinusoidal trajectory more
accurately with a smaller control input.

\label{tab:sine}

FOPID           & $8.29 \times 10^{-3}$ & $2.41 \times 10^{4}$ & 4.74\\
FOPSO-GWO-FOPID & $\mathbf{1.88 \times 10^{-3}}$ & $\mathbf{9.61 \times 10^{3}}$ & \textbf{1.72}\\

\section{Conclusion}

This paper studied the trajectory tracking control of a 6-DOF robotic arm with FOPID
controllers and proposed FOPSO-GWO, a hybrid of fractional-order PSO and the grey wolf
optimizer, to tune their 30 parameters. The fractional-order velocity keeps a memory of the
particles' previous motion, and the grey wolf mechanism guides the search with the three
best solutions. The fitness function evaluates the step and sinusoidal responses of all
joints and limits the driving torque and overshoot of each joint. Simulation results show
that, compared with PID and FOPID control, the FOPID controller tuned by FOPSO-GWO has
smaller overshoot, shorter adjustment and peak times and a smaller tracking error, which
meets the high-precision control requirements of the 6-DOF robotic arm. Future work will
verify the method on a physical robotic arm.
